title: Organ Signature Antibodies: TSH Receptor, Gastric, Insulin and Myasthenia Serology
summary: Learn what TSH receptor, parietal cell, intrinsic factor, insulin and myasthenia gravis antibody tests can and cannot show: binding versus functional TSH receptor assays, sensitive versus specific gastric antibodies, why insulin autoantibodies must be drawn before insulin, and what to do when acetylcholine receptor antibody is negative.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 55 Hits 9 (AChR/MuSK in myasthenia gravis), 14 (Graves: TSI vs TBII) and 15 (pernicious anaemia PCA vs IFA), and Trap 4 (IAA in a long-treated diabetic), checked against Kahaly and Diana 2017, Diana 2018, Furmaniak 2013, Vargas-Uricoechea 2023, Rustgi 2021, Andres and Serraj 2012, Iwamuro 2023, Kawasaki 2023, the Sacks 2011 laboratory guideline and the Sacks 2023 update (read via a page-fetch tool), and Lazaridis and Tzartos 2020. Qualified: the reviewer’s “~5% double-negative” and “30–40% MuSK of the remainder” differ from the review read (about 10% seronegative on classical assays; MuSK about 40% of AChR-negative, lower in Japan; AChR sensitivity about 50% in ocular MG) (register flag rv-mg-seronegative-fraction); “atrophic = TSI-negative” is qualified because stimulating and blocking antibodies can coexist (rv-graves-tsi-atrophic-coexist). Qualified: the “>14 days” IAA cut-off is taught as “before insulin starts” with the guideline’s about 11 days to antibody induction (register flag rv-iaa-insulin-induction-days). Pending and not taught: the exact 14-day cut-off, exogenous insulin antibodies “running much higher”, PCA falling to 55% in advanced disease, IFA types, transplacental neonatal MG.

objectives: Explain why a TSH receptor binding assay (TBII) cannot distinguish stimulating from blocking antibodies.
Compare the sensitivity and specificity of parietal cell and intrinsic factor antibodies.
Explain why insulin autoantibodies must be measured before insulin treatment.
State the approximate frequencies of AChR, MuSK and seronegative myasthenia gravis and the next test after a negative AChR antibody.

scenes.title: Four positives, four questions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four requests. (1) A woman with hyperthyroidism and bulging eyes: TSH receptor binding assay (TBII) positive; (2) an older adult with macrocytic anaemia: parietal cell antibody (PCA) positive, intrinsic factor antibody (IFA) negative; (3) a man on insulin for three years: insulin autoantibody (IAA) requested to "confirm type 1"; (4) a woman with fatigable drooping eyelids: acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody negative. Question token: “What does each result really prove?”

cues.text: Four invented requests. A woman with hyperthyroidism and bulging eyes has a positive TSH receptor binding assay. An older adult with macrocytic anaemia is parietal cell antibody positive, intrinsic factor antibody negative.
A man on insulin for three years has insulin autoantibodies ordered to confirm type 1 diabetes. And a woman with drooping eyelids that worsen with use is acetylcholine receptor antibody negative.
What does each result really prove, and what can it not tell you?

scenes.title: One organ, one target
scenes.altText: Schematic: four target cards. Thyroid: antibodies to the TSH receptor; stimulating antibodies (TSAb/TSI) activate it and cause Graves hyperthyroidism and its extrathyroidal signs, blocking antibodies (TBAb) bind without activating and can cause hypothyroidism. Stomach: parietal cell antibodies target the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump; intrinsic factor antibodies target the vitamin B12 carrier. Islet: insulin, GAD65, IA-2 and ZnT8 autoantibodies. Neuromuscular junction: AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies.

cues.text: Each organ has its own target. In the thyroid it is the TSH receptor. Stimulating antibodies switch it on and cause Graves disease, including the eye signs. Blocking antibodies bind it without switching it on and can cause hypothyroidism.
In the stomach, parietal cell antibodies target the proton pump, and intrinsic factor antibodies target the protein needed to absorb vitamin B12.
In the pancreatic islets, autoantibodies to insulin, GAD65, IA-2 and zinc transporter 8 mark autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
At the neuromuscular junction, myasthenia gravis antibodies target the acetylcholine receptor, or, less often, MuSK or LRP4.

scenes.title: What the assay cannot see
scenes.altText: Three assay cards. TSH receptor: TBII is a competitive binding assay — both stimulating and blocking antibodies inhibit TSH binding, so TBII measures total binding, not function; cell-based bioassays (cAMP) separate stimulating (TSAb/TSI) from blocking (TBAb). Gastric: PCA is sensitive (about 85–90% of autoimmune gastritis) but not specific (also in Helicobacter pylori infection and other autoimmune disease) and declines with age; IFA is highly specific but only about 50% sensitive in pernicious anaemia. Insulin: insulin antibodies develop after insulin therapy, even with human insulin, and the radioassay cannot tell them from autoantibodies — measure IAA before insulin starts; a laboratory guideline states insulin treatment precludes IAA analysis because insulin antibodies are induced in about 11 days.

cues.text: Now the catch. The common TSH receptor test, TBII, is a binding assay. Stimulating and blocking antibodies both stop TSH from binding, so TBII measures binding, not function. Only a cell-based bioassay separates stimulating from blocking antibodies.

Parietal cell antibodies are sensitive, found in about eighty-five to ninety percent of autoimmune gastritis, but not specific: they also occur with Helicobacter pylori and other autoimmune diseases, and they fall with age. Intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific, but found in only about half of pernicious anaemia.
Insulin autoantibodies have a timing problem. Anyone given insulin, even human insulin, can make insulin antibodies, and the assay cannot tell those from autoantibodies.

So insulin autoantibodies should be measured before insulin treatment starts. A laboratory guideline says insulin treatment rules out the test, because insulin antibodies are induced in about eleven days. One study accepted samples only up to two weeks after insulin was started.

scenes.title: Myasthenia serology, and the hook answers
scenes.altText: MG serology card (Lazaridis and Tzartos 2020): AChR antibodies in about 85% of MG overall; the radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) is about 99% specific, about 85% sensitive in generalised and about 50% in ocular MG. MuSK antibodies in about 6% of all MG, about 40% of AChR-negative patients (less common in Japan), mainly IgG4. LRP4 about 2%. About 10% have no antibody on classical AChR and MuSK assays (seronegative); cell-based assays find antibodies in some of them. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Myasthenia gravis serology. About eighty-five percent of patients have acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The standard assay is about ninety-nine percent specific, but sensitivity is about eighty-five percent in generalised disease and only about half in ocular disease.

MuSK antibodies are found in about six percent of all patients, about forty percent of those without receptor antibodies, and are mostly IgG4. LRP4 antibodies are rarer. About ten percent have no antibody on the classical assays.

Back to the hook. A positive TBII fits Graves disease in a hyperthyroid patient with eye signs, but by itself it cannot show stimulation. The positive parietal cell antibody is sensitive but not specific, and a negative intrinsic factor antibody does not exclude pernicious anaemia.
Insulin autoantibodies after three years of insulin cannot be interpreted. And a negative receptor antibody does not rule out myasthenia: test for MuSK next.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A positive TBII proves stimulating antibodies” (✓ binding assays detect stimulating and blocking antibodies; a bioassay measures function); “A positive PCA confirms pernicious anaemia” (✓ PCA is sensitive but nonspecific; IFA is the specific marker); “Positive IAA in a long-treated diabetic confirms type 1” (✓ insulin therapy induces insulin antibodies; measure before insulin).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive TBII proves stimulating antibodies. No: the binding assay also detects blocking antibodies. Only a bioassay shows function.
Trap two: a positive parietal cell antibody confirms pernicious anaemia. No: it is sensitive but not specific. Intrinsic factor antibody is the specific marker.
Trap three: positive insulin autoantibodies in a long-treated diabetic confirm type 1. No: insulin treatment itself induces insulin antibodies.

props.title: ✗ “PCA + = pernicious anaemia.”
lines: ✓ Sensitive, not specific; IFA is specific

scenes.title: Foot, alarm, marshal, stopwatch
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “TBII sees a FOOT on the pedal but not whether it is the gas or the brake. PCA is the SMOKE ALARM: rings early and often, sometimes for toast. IFA is the FIRE MARSHAL: rarely wrong, often not there yet. IAA runs on a STOPWATCH that starts with the first insulin dose.” Tokens: foot = TBII · alarm = PCA · marshal = IFA · stopwatch = IAA. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: TBII sees a foot on the pedal, but not whether it is the gas or the brake. Parietal cell antibody is the smoke alarm: it rings early, sometimes for burnt toast. Intrinsic factor antibody is the fire marshal: rarely wrong, often absent. Insulin autoantibodies run on a stopwatch that starts with the first insulin dose.

Where it breaks: stimulating and blocking antibodies can coexist in one patient; parietal cell antibodies fall with age, so the alarm can go quiet; and myasthenia antibody rates depend on the assay and the population.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “TBII = binding, not function · PCA sensitive, IFA specific”, “IAA before insulin · AChR negative → test MuSK”.

cues.text: A TSH receptor binding assay cannot tell stimulating from blocking antibodies, parietal cell antibodies are sensitive while intrinsic factor antibodies are specific, insulin autoantibodies belong before insulin treatment, and a negative acetylcholine receptor antibody does not exclude myasthenia gravis.

props.label: TBII = binding, not function · PCA sensitive, IFA specific
IAA before insulin · AChR negative → test MuSK

explanation.what: Plain language: in organ-specific autoimmunity each organ has its own antibody target, but each test has a blind spot. Some tests see that an antibody binds but not what it does; some are sensitive but nonspecific; one is spoiled by treatment; and one is negative in a sizeable minority of real cases. Scientific terms: TSH receptor antibody (TRAb), TSH-binding inhibitory immunoglobulin (TBII), thyroid-stimulating antibody or immunoglobulin (TSAb/TSI), TSH receptor blocking antibody (TBAb), cell-based bioassay (cAMP), parietal cell antibody (PCA; H+/K+ ATPase), intrinsic factor antibody (IFA), autoimmune gastritis, insulin autoantibody (IAA), GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, acetylcholine receptor (AChR), muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), LRP4, radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA), cell-based assay, seronegative myasthenia gravis.
explanation.why: Stimulating and blocking TSH receptor antibodies both inhibit TSH binding; PCA also occurs in Helicobacter pylori infection and other autoimmune disease; insulin therapy induces insulin antibodies, in about 11 days by one guideline, that the IAA assay cannot distinguish from autoantibodies; and some myasthenia patients have antibodies to other junction proteins, or levels below the detection limit of classical assays.
explanation.measure: TBII = total binding; bioassay separates TSAb from TBAb. PCA about 85–90% sensitive in autoimmune gastritis, not specific, declines with age; IFA highly specific, about 50% sensitive in pernicious anaemia (ELISA figures in one review: IFA about 37% sensitive, 100% specific; PCA about 81.5% sensitive, 90.3% specific). IAA: measure before insulin starts — a laboratory guideline states insulin treatment precludes IAA analysis because insulin antibodies are induced in about 11 days (one study accepted samples up to 2 weeks after starting). MG: AChR about 85% overall (RIPA about 99% specific; about 85% sensitive generalised, about 50% ocular); MuSK about 6% overall, about 40% of AChR-negative, mostly IgG4; LRP4 about 2%; about 10% seronegative on classical assays.
explanation.differs: TBII (binding) vs TSAb/TSI and TBAb bioassays (function); PCA (sensitive) vs IFA (specific); IAA in insulin-naive vs insulin-treated patients; AChR-positive vs MuSK-positive vs seronegative myasthenia gravis.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the test that proves stimulating activity, pick the more specific antibody for pernicious anaemia, reject an IAA result in an insulin-treated patient, or choose MuSK testing after a negative AChR antibody.

questions.stem: A hyperthyroid patient has a positive TSH receptor antibody by a competitive binding (TBII) assay. Which test shows whether the antibody is stimulating rather than blocking?

options.text: A cell-based TSH receptor bioassay measuring cAMP
options.rationale: Correct. Bioassays measure receptor function and separate stimulating (TSAb/TSI) from blocking (TBAb) antibodies.

options.text: Repeating the TBII assay at a higher dilution
options.rationale: Incorrect. TBII measures binding inhibition at any dilution; stimulating and blocking antibodies both inhibit TSH binding.
Incorrect. IFA is a gastric autoantibody of pernicious anaemia, unrelated to the TSH receptor.
Incorrect. Free T4 does not identify the antibody type, and stimulating and blocking antibodies can coexist in one patient.

questions.stem: For suspected pernicious anaemia, which statement about gastric autoantibodies is correct?

options.text: Intrinsic factor antibody is highly specific but detected in only about half of patients
options.rationale: Correct. IFA is highly specific, with sensitivity of about 50% in pernicious anaemia.

options.text: Parietal cell antibody is highly specific for pernicious anaemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. PCA is sensitive but also occurs in Helicobacter pylori infection and other autoimmune diseases.

options.text: A negative intrinsic factor antibody excludes pernicious anaemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. With about 50% sensitivity, a negative IFA does not exclude it.

options.text: Parietal cell antibody becomes more reliable with increasing age
options.rationale: Incorrect. PCA declines with age and may be less reliable from about age 50.

questions.stem: A woman with fatigable ptosis and limb weakness has a negative acetylcholine receptor antibody by radioimmunoprecipitation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Testing for MuSK antibodies is appropriate; about 40% of AChR-negative patients have them
options.rationale: Correct. MuSK antibodies are found in about 40% of AChR antibody-negative myasthenia gravis.
Incorrect. About 15% of patients lack AChR antibodies on classical assays, and sensitivity is lower in ocular disease.

options.text: Insulin autoantibodies should be tested next
options.rationale: Incorrect. IAA is a type 1 diabetes marker, unrelated to the neuromuscular junction.

options.text: MuSK antibodies, if present, are mainly complement-fixing IgG1
options.rationale: Incorrect. MuSK antibodies are mainly IgG4, which does not activate complement.

Insulin antibodies develop following insulin therapy even in those people who use human insulin; insulin treatment precludes the analysis of IAA as it takes only about 11 days before insulin antibodies are induced.

claims.text: TBII is a binding assay positive with stimulating or blocking antibodies; bioassays separate TSAb/TSI from TBAb; stimulating antibodies cause Graves hyperthyroidism and extrathyroidal signs; blocking antibodies can cause hypothyroidism; the two can coexist.
PCA (H+/K+ ATPase) about 85–90% sensitive, not specific, declines with age; IFA highly specific, about 50% sensitive in pernicious anaemia.

Insulin therapy induces insulin antibodies indistinguishable from IAA by the assay, even with human insulin; measure IAA before insulin starts — a guideline states antibodies are induced in about 11 days, and one study accepted samples only from insulin-naive patients or within 2 weeks of starting.
Islet autoantibodies: insulin, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8.
AChR about 85% (RIPA ~99% specific; ~85% generalised, ~50% ocular); MuSK ~6% overall, ~40% of AChR-negative, mainly IgG4; LRP4 ~2%; ~10% seronegative on classical assays.
Reviewer: the exact 14-day IAA cut-off; exogenous insulin antibodies “run much higher”; PCA 55% in advanced disease; IFA blocking (I) and binding (II) types; neonatal MG transplacental and transient.
claims.note: Not taught. The 14-day figure itself was not found in the sources read: Sacks 2023 gives about 11 days to antibody induction and Kawasaki 2023 uses 2 weeks as a study inclusion rule, so the lesson teaches those sourced numbers instead. The other items were not confirmed in the sources read.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 55 Hit 9 gives AChR antibodies in 85–90% of MG, anti-MuSK in 30–40% of the remainder and about 5% double-negative. The MuSK fraction agrees with Lazaridis and Tzartos 2020 (about 6% of all MG, about 40% of patients without AChR antibodies), but the two reviews put AChR at about 85% (80–85% by RIPA) and the seronegative fraction at about 10%, not about 5%, on the classical AChR and MuSK assays. The hit also omits that AChR sensitivity is about 85% in generalised but only about 50% in ocular MG, that MuSK is less common in Japanese patients (2–3%), and that cell-based assays find antibodies in some seronegative patients. The lesson teaches the review figures and that rates depend on assay and population (register flag rv-mg-seronegative-fraction).

Ch. 55 Hit 14 states atrophic thyroiditis is TSI-negative. Sources read describe blocking antibodies in atrophic thyroiditis but also show stimulating and blocking antibodies coexisting in one patient (Furmaniak 2013) and TBAb with TSAb in patients with alternating thyroid function and atrophic thyroiditis (Vargas-Uricoechea 2023). The lesson teaches that TBII cannot separate the two and that they can coexist (register flag rv-graves-tsi-atrophic-coexist).

Ch. 55 Hit 10 and Trap 4 set the cut-off at “more than 14 days” of insulin, and the chapter’s memory hook calls it a “14-day insulin amnesia”. The 2023 laboratory guideline read gives a shorter interval: insulin treatment precludes the analysis of IAA because it takes only about 11 days before insulin antibodies are induced, and Kawasaki 2023 counted IAA only in insulin-naive patients or those within 2 weeks of starting insulin. A fixed 14-day window is therefore more permissive than the guideline; the lesson teaches “before insulin starts” with the about 11-day figure (register flag rv-iaa-insulin-induction-days).

Citations re-verified against Europe PMC; Sacks 2023 was reachable only through a page-fetch tool. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
